opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that you can't just put people from different fields in the same building and hope something magical happens. Proximity helps, but it's not sufficient. What we've tried to do at Arc is design the structure around problems rather than around departments.

Traditional academia is organized by discipline. You have a biology department, a computer science department, a chemistry department, and each has its own incentives, its own journals, its own way of deciding who gets tenure. So even when people want to collaborate, the system quietly pulls them back into their silos. A computational person helping a wet lab gets a middle-authorship paper that doesn't count much for their career, and vice versa.

At Arc, we have a few things that work together. First, our core investigators get long-term, flexible funding, so they're not spending their time writing grants for narrowly scoped projects. That gives them room to take risks and to work on things that sit between fields. Second, we've built technology centers, shared platforms in areas like genome engineering, cell biology, multi-omics, and machine learning, staffed by professional scientists and engineers. They're not just service cores. They're partners who build capabilities that no single lab could build on its own.

Third, and this has become more important over time, we organize around a few big, concrete goals. The virtual cell is a good example. If your goal is to build models that can predict how a cell responds to perturbations, you need people who can generate massive, high-quality perturbation datasets, people who can build foundation models, and people who understand the biology deeply enough to ask the right questions and tell you when the model is wrong. The shared goal is what forces the integration. Nobody can do it alone, so the collaboration isn't optional.

Culturally, I think the key is mutual respect and a shared language. We want biologists who are comfortable with computation and machine learning people who actually care about biology, not just using it as another benchmark. That takes time. You have to let people fail together a bit and learn how the other side thinks. But when it works, you get this tight loop between experiment and computation, where the model tells you what experiment to run next, and the experiment tells you where the model is broken. That loop is what we're really trying to build.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the founding premise of Arc was really that the most interesting problems in biology today don't sit cleanly inside any one department. If you want to actually understand something like a complex disease, you need people who can build the measurement tools, people who can generate data at scale, people who can model it computationally, and people who understand the underlying biology deeply enough to ask the right questions in the first place. And historically, those people have lived in different buildings, on different grant cycles, with different incentive structures.

So the first thing we did was structural. We give our core investigators long-term, no-strings funding, so they're not spending half their time writing grants that force them to narrow their work into something a study section recognizes. That frees people up to wander into adjacent fields, which is where a lot of the real progress happens.

The second piece is that we built what we call technology centers, which are essentially shared platforms run by professional scientists and engineers rather than rotating trainees. So if a lab wants to do a massive perturbation screen or build a virtual cell model, they don't have to reinvent that capability from scratch. The expertise is already there, and it's maintained. That lowers the activation energy for a wet-lab biologist to work with machine learning folks and vice versa.

And then honestly, a lot of it is just culture and physical proximity. We put computational people and experimentalists in the same space, we hire people who are genuinely curious about the other side, and we try to reward collaboration rather than treating it as something you do after you've secured your own credit. When a machine learning researcher is sitting next to someone who's actually running the experiments, they develop intuitions about what the data really means, and the experimentalist starts to think about how to design experiments that are useful for training models. That feedback loop is hard to get any other way.

So I'd say it's less about forcing disciplines together and more about removing the friction that normally keeps them apart, and then letting good people find each other.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is a shared scientific question. You can put biologists, computer scientists, and engineers in the same building, but that alone doesn’t create collaboration. They need a problem that they’re excited about and that none of them can solve on their own.

Then you need time to develop a shared language. Different fields have different intuitions about what constitutes a good experiment or convincing evidence. Making those assumptions explicit is really valuable. Ideally, that interaction happens early enough that people shape the question together, rather than one discipline handing another a finished problem to analyze.

That’s the kind of environment we want to build at Arc: one where learning from another field is part of doing the science.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it starts with bringing people together around a shared scientific question. Biology gives us incredibly rich problems, and answering them often requires experimentalists, computational scientists, and engineers to work closely together.

The challenge is that different fields have different languages and intuitions about what matters. So you need time to build trust, ask basic questions, and understand one another’s constraints. You want that exchange to shape the project from the beginning, because someone from another discipline can change how you frame the question itself.

At Arc, the approach is to create conditions where those collaborations can develop: give people room to explore, make it easy to work together, and keep the focus on the scientific problem rather than disciplinary boundaries.
